title: SAUL AND DAVID: JEALOUSY WILL MAKE YOU ATTACK PEOPLE GOD NEVER CALLED YOUR ENEMIES
paragraphs: SAUL AND DAVID: JEALOUSY WILL MAKE YOU ATTACK PEOPLE GOD NEVER CALLED YOUR ENEMIES
The most dangerous spear may not come from someone who hates God. Sometimes it comes from someone who once loved you—until your grace exposed what they were afraid of losing.
David was playing the harp when the spear came flying.
Read that again.
He was not attacking Saul.
He was not organizing a rebellion.
He was not standing outside the palace demanding Saul's throne.
He was serving him.
And Saul tried to kill him.

There is something deeply disturbing about that scene because it reveals how jealousy can corrupt the way we see people. It can take someone God sent to bless us and convince us that they are a threat. It can turn friendship into suspicion, admiration into resentment, and insecurity into hostility.
And perhaps the frightening question is not whether you have ever met a Saul.
Perhaps the frightening question is whether Saul has ever been living inside you.
Because jealousy rarely introduces itself by saying, I am jealous.
It usually sounds much more reasonable.
“Something about that person bothers me.”
“They're getting too much attention.”
“I don't trust their motives.”
“Everybody acts like they're so special.”
“They haven't earned what they have.”
“Why does everything seem to work for them?”
And beneath all those sentences may be a wound we are terrified to admit:
Why them, God?
That is where Saul's tragedy begins to become painfully personal.
Before David became a fugitive running through wilderness caves, he was the young shepherd who stepped onto a battlefield while seasoned soldiers were terrified of Goliath.
David's confidence was not ultimately confidence in David.
It was confidence in God.
He told the Philistine:
“I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts.”
—1 Samuel 17:45
The Hebrew expression translated “LORD of hosts” is יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת — YHWH Tseva'ot, carrying the sense of the LORD of armies or hosts.
David understood something Goliath did not.
The shepherd boy was not standing there alone.
This battle belonged to God.
David defeated Goliath, and Israel celebrated.
That should have been good news for Saul.
His enemy had been defeated.
His army had been delivered.
His kingdom had benefited.
David's victory was not Saul's loss.
But jealousy has a terrifying ability to interpret someone else's blessing as your subtraction.
When the women celebrated Israel's victory, they sang:
“Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
—1 Samuel 18:7
Then Scripture records the sentence that opened the door to Saul's downward spiral:
“And Saul was very angry.”
—1 Samuel 18:8
Why?
Because comparison had entered the room.
Saul heard David's praise and interpreted it as Saul's humiliation.
He essentially asked what David could have left to gain except the kingdom.
Then comes one of the most revealing lines in the entire story:
“And Saul eyed David from that day on.”
—1 Samuel 18:9
The Hebrew behind the idea of Saul “eyeing” David is associated with עָוַן — ʿāwan, conveying the sense here of watching suspiciously or regarding someone with distrust.
Something had changed.
Not David.
Saul's eyes.
Yesterday David was useful.
Today David was dangerous.
Yesterday his music brought Saul relief.
Today his existence made Saul insecure.
Yesterday David's courage saved Israel.
Today David's success felt threatening.
That is what unchecked jealousy does.
It does not merely change how you feel about someone.
It changes how you see them.
Suddenly their success looks arrogant.
Their confidence looks prideful.
Their opportunities look undeserved.
Their testimony irritates you.
Their influence bothers you.
Their happiness feels almost offensive.
Their progress becomes evidence in an imaginary case you have been building against them.
And sometimes they have done absolutely nothing to you.
They simply possess something you wish you had.
That is when jealousy becomes spiritually dangerous.
Because you may begin fighting someone God never declared your enemy.
Scripture says:
“And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him.”
—1 Samuel 18:14
That was the real issue.
David carried something Saul desperately wanted to control but could not manufacture:
the favor and presence of God.
Saul could wear the crown.
David could carry God's favor.
Saul could occupy the palace.
David could walk in God's purpose.
And Saul slowly became more concerned about preserving his position than surrendering himself to God.
So David played his instrument.
Saul held his spear.
Think about that picture.
One man was using his gift to soothe the suffering of another.
The other was holding a weapon against the person serving him.
Then:
“Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear.”
—1 Samuel 19:10
David escaped.
But the spear tells us something.
Jealousy does not remain a private emotion forever.
If continually fed, it eventually searches for a weapon.
Maybe yours is not made of wood and iron.
Maybe your spear is gossip.
Maybe it is sarcasm.
Maybe it is a carefully worded Facebook post designed so everyone knows exactly who you mean without you mentioning their name.
Maybe it is withholding encouragement.
Maybe it is secretly celebrating when someone fails.
Maybe it is discrediting another person's ministry because theirs is growing.
Maybe it is poisoning someone's reputation because their gift makes you feel invisible.
Maybe it is refusing to support a friend because you cannot tolerate watching them succeed before you.
Maybe it is calling something “discernment” when deep inside you know it is envy.
This is where Scripture becomes uncomfortable.
Because the Bible does not allow us to treat jealousy as harmless.
Proverbs 14:30 says:
“A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.”
James goes even further:
“For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.”
—James 3:16
The Greek word translated “jealousy” or “bitter jealousy” in this context is ζῆλος — zēlos.
The word can describe zeal, but context determines whether that zeal is rightly directed or corrupted. In James 3, it is explicitly joined with selfish ambition and contrasted with wisdom from above.
That matters.
Because passion is not automatically holiness.
Intensity is not automatically righteousness.
You can feel strongly and still be wrong.
You can be convinced someone is your enemy while your real enemy is the jealousy growing inside your own heart.
And Saul kept feeding it.
David became successful.
Saul became afraid.
David behaved wisely.
Saul became suspicious.
David gained affection from the people.
Saul became more threatened.
And eventually Saul spent enormous energy hunting the very man who repeatedly refused to destroy him.
That is the insanity of jealousy.
It can make you waste years fighting imaginary wars.
You lose sleep over people who are not thinking about you.
You interpret their silence.
You analyze their posts.
You monitor their progress.
You compare numbers.
You compare marriages.
You compare ministries.
You compare bodies.
You compare houses.
You compare careers.
You compare children.
You compare followers.
You compare testimonies.
You compare blessings.
And while staring at someone else's life, you slowly stop stewarding your own.
Saul became obsessed with David.
David remained occupied with God.
And there came a moment when the roles were reversed.
David had the opportunity to kill Saul.
Saul entered a cave where David and his men were hiding.
David's men essentially told him, This is your chance.
Imagine the temptation.
The man hunting you is suddenly vulnerable.
The person who threw spears at you is within reach.
The king who forced you from your home is defenseless.
David could have called revenge justice.
He could have called murder destiny.
He could have interpreted opportunity as permission.
Instead, David refused.
He said:
“The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed.”
—1 Samuel 24:6
David understood something many wounded people forget:
Someone else's sin does not give you permission to become sinful.
Saul's spear did not justify David's knife.
That sentence may be for someone reading this with tears behind their eyes.
You were betrayed.
You were lied about.
You were humiliated.
Someone became jealous of you and tried to destroy your name.
Someone you helped turned against you.
Someone you defended became the person attacking you.
Someone took your kindness and answered it with cruelty.
Your pain is real.
But Jesus is not calling you to become the person who wounded you.
Do not let another person's bitterness reproduce itself inside you.
Do not carry Saul's spear simply because Saul threw it first.
David's restraint was not weakness.
It was evidence that David trusted God with justice.
And eventually the contrast between Saul and David becomes heartbreaking.
One man was desperately trying to keep a kingdom.
The other was learning how to surrender his future to God.
One grasped.
One waited.
One hunted.
One trusted.
One became consumed with another man's calling.
The other learned to survive caves without abandoning his God.
But we must be careful here.
David was not the perfect hero.
If we stop the story at David's noblest moments, we miss the Gospel.
Because David himself would later fall catastrophically.
The man who refused to murder Saul would eventually arrange circumstances leading to Uriah's death after committing adultery with Bathsheba.
David needed mercy too.
That is why the Bible is not ultimately a collection of stories about good people defeating bad people.
It is the story of sinful humanity desperately needing a perfect King.
Saul cannot save us.
David cannot save us.
Only Jesus can.
And this is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Because generations after David, another King came.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of David.
The King David could only foreshadow.
He had no sinful jealousy.
No selfish ambition.
No corrupt throne to protect.
No insecurity.
No hidden rebellion against the Father.
Jesus was betrayed by someone close to Him.
Accused falsely.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Spat upon.
Stripped.
Crucified.
And unlike David, Jesus did not merely spare the life of an enemy.
Jesus gave His life for His enemies.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
And Romans 5:10 says that we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies.
There is the Gospel.
We were not merely Davids being hunted by Sauls.
In our sin, we were rebels against God.
We have envied.
Compared.
Resented.
Gossiped.
Hated.
Coveted.
Judged.
Competed.
Wounded.
Hidden.
And Christ went to the cross for sinners like us.
The answer to jealousy is therefore deeper than telling yourself, Stop comparing.
You need a new heart.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need Jesus.
Because when your identity becomes rooted in Christ, another person's blessing no longer has to feel like God's rejection of you.
Their calling does not cancel yours.
Their testimony does not erase yours.
Their opportunity does not prove God forgot you.
Their beauty does not diminish your worth.
Their ministry does not make yours meaningless.
Their success does not mean heaven has run out of grace.
You do not have to throw spears at people because God placed something beautiful in their hands.
You can celebrate them.
You can pray for them.
You can bless them.
You can say, “Father, thank You for what You are doing in their life. Keep my heart clean.”
And perhaps that prayer is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Because there is a name in your mind right now.
You know it.
The person whose success stings.
The person whose posts you sometimes cannot stand seeing.
The person you secretly compare yourself with.
The person whose failure would give a dark corner of your heart a little satisfaction.
Do not excuse it.
Bring it into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Repentance does not begin when you become impressive.
Repentance begins when you stop hiding.
Tell Him:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have been comparing. I have been jealous. I have allowed someone else's blessing to become bitterness in me. Clean my heart. Teach me to love what You are doing in other people without believing You have forgotten me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the struggle is not there.

And maybe somebody else reading your comment needs to discover that Christians do not have to pretend they never struggle—we bring our darkness to Jesus because His grace is greater than what we have hidden.
Not because what happened was acceptable.
Not because forgiveness means pretending there was no wound.
But because you refuse to let their spear become your identity.
Jesus can heal what they damaged without turning you into what damaged you.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.

But if this truth can interrupt one person's jealousy before it destroys a friendship, one marriage, one family, one church, or one calling, sharing it becomes a simple opportunity to put biblical truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Send this privately to the person exhausted from comparison.
Your support can help this ministry place more Gospel-centered material before believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and people who may not yet know Christ.
Come to Jesus.
A ministry cannot cleanse your heart.
A Christian product cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus Christ can.
The same Gospel that confronts the Saul hiding in us also offers mercy to the Saul hiding in us.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Lay down the spear.
Stop treating God's children as competitors.
Stop measuring your worth against somebody else's calling.
Stop letting comparison rob you of gratitude.
Stop demanding somebody else's light become dimmer before you believe God can still use yours.
There is room in the kingdom for obedience without rivalry.
There is grace enough to celebrate another person's victory.
There is healing for the person who has been hunted.
There is forgiveness for the person who has done the hunting.
And there is a King greater than Saul, greater than David, greater than every throne we have ever fought to protect.
His name is Jesus.
Maybe the greatest victory in your life will not be proving your enemies wrong.
Maybe it will be discovering that some of the people you were fighting were never your enemies at all.
And maybe tonight, Jesus is asking you to finally put the spear down.
Because when grace takes hold of the hand that once held the spear, the story does not have to end in scandal.
